name: Silver Grey
lede: Silver grey is a cool, slightly bluish mid-grey, named for the metal and an old standard in grey vocabularies.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines silver grey as a bluish grey [1]. The metal itself in the X11 color set, called silver, is a lighter, neutral grey with hex code #C0C0C0 [2]. The swatch here is a darker, cooler grey with a tint of blue [3]. In the ISCC-NBS system it falls near a pale blue, 5.3 units from the swatch [3]. It was already a standard name in Ridgway's color list of 1912 and the RAL list of 1927 [3].

A pipe-marking code described in the same dictionary gives silver-grey to steam [4]. Its siblings in the neutrals are [[silver]], [[pearl-grey]], [[slate-grey]], [[steel-grey]] and [[gunmetal]] [3].

sections.title: Averages are grey
sections.body:
Ball tells of Sherrie Levine's *Melt-Down* paintings of 1990, monochromes made by averaging the colors of famous works by computer [5]. The average of a Monet comes out as a darkish silver-grey [5]. Ball reads that lack of any hue as a sign of how wide a spectrum Monet's work covers [5].

Even a living thing can be this color. Greenfield notes that a wild cochineal insect ranges in color from silver-grey to red-black [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Silver grey is a common painted color. In our archive of 23,781 paintings it appears in 527, 2.22 per cent, and is more common than 74 per cent of the named colors [7]. It most often plays a light, the lit part of a scene (50 per cent of 257 works measured) [7]. Alfred Sisley uses it in 8 of his 50 archive paintings, about seven times the baseline rate, and Monet in 5 of 50, about four times [7]. It peaks in the 1900s with 1.7 per cent of 1,674 paintings, only 1.4 times the baseline [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [7]. In Google Books the term rises from about 1870 and peaks near 1920 [8].
